All samples possess a north and downward directed component in geographic coordinates at temperatures up to 660°C that is ascribed to a Cretaceous overprint. Two components isolated above 660°C reveal distinct directional clusters: one is interpreted as a depositional remanence, while the other appears to be the result of a mid‐Paleozoic (460 to 420 Ma) remagnetization, which is likely widespread throughout South China. Low Temperature Experiments Low temperature experiments were performed on the VSM using a liquid nitrogen cryostat (Figure S1 in Sup- porting Information S1 ). A magnetizing field of 1.8 T was applied at room temperature (293 K) then switched off. Magnetic remanence was then measured in a null field down to 100 K and then upon warming to room tem- perature at a rate of 0.25°/s. Pure hematite typically shows a drop in remanence through the Morin transition (Özdemir et al., 2008 ) around ∼ 250 K; however, none of the Yangjiaping samples displayed either a measurable Morin transition or a Verwey transition (characteristic of magnetite), at least until 100 K (note that temperature stability of the cryostat decreases approaching 100 K). Dekkers and Linssen ( 1989 ) observed similar low tem- perature behavior in natural hematite and suggested that impurities (e.g., adsorbed silica) might suppress the Morin transition. Interpretation and Discussion Our experimental results offer several insights into the nature of the remanent magnetizations in the Laoshanya Formation: 1. SEM analyses show that group C samples contain abundant detrital (ca. 30–100 μm) Ti‐rich hematite grains indicative of MD grain sizes, consistent with an igneous or metamorphic source (Basu & Molinaroli, 1989 ), and therefore a primary /detrital remanence (DRM). These samples also contain a reduced presence of < 1– 2 μm (SD‐sized) hematite flakes relative to the samples from groups A and B. Hysteresis curves for group C samples appear wasp‐waisted, indicating distinct magnetic populations or dominantly MD grains. Thermal‐ susceptibility curves for group C also showed minor to non‐existent Hopkinson peaks, consistent with MD behavior. 2. Previous Paleomagnetic/Polarity Stratigraphy Studies In a regional study of Permian age sedimentary rocks in the American Southwest, Peterson and Nairn (1971) reported data from one site in what they referred to as the Dewey Lake Formation, exposed near Carlsbad, New Mexico. The NRM of the volcanic samples were measured using an AGICO JR6 spinner magnetometer, while sedimentary samples were measured using a 2G-755 cryogenic magnetome- ter. Characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) directions and site-mean directions were determined using principal component analysis (Kirschvink 1980 ) and Fisher ( 1953 ) statistics. Different magnetic components were determined based on well-deﬁned lin- ear segments including at least three demagnetization steps on the orthogonal vector diagram, with the maximum angular devi- ation (MAD) < 15 ◦. Any outliers of the isolated ChRM directions that deviated far from the site average were excluded from further calculations. 4. Mesozoic strata include Jurassic, Cretaceous and Cenozoic continental clastic rocks (BGMRQP 1991 ). Fortunately, Triassic volcanic rocks are exposed at the eastern and southern edges of the block. The western expo- sure is in the Qimantagh region, and it comprises mainly Upper Triassic continental volcanic rocks, including brick red, dark pur- ple or grey rhyolites interbedded with dacite that unconformably overlie the underlying strata. The eastern exposure is in the Dulan area and comprises mainly andesites and interbedded dacite tuff and tuff breccias (Fig. 1 b, BGMRQP 1991 ). These volcanic rocks oc- cur along the Permian–Triassic Eastern Kunlun–Qaidam magmatic belt and are considered to have originated from subduction and the collision of the Palaeo-Tethyan Ocean basin (Chen et al. 2010 , 2015 ). Th is note aims to study the kinematics characteristics of intracontinental blocks in eastern China since the Mesozoic by means of paleomag- netism. 1 Geological settings and sample collection Eastern China underwent frequent intensive volcanic eruptions resulting from a complex influence of the west- ern Pacific plate and deep Earth’s processes during the middle to late Mesozoic. The age of the Tiaojishan Formation volcanics was recently dated from 153 Ma to 161 Ma by U –Pb and 40Ar–39Ar. A total of 154 samples from 16 sites within the Tiaojishan Formation were collected. Geological setting and paleomagnetic sampling The Chengde basin is geologically located in the southern margin of the Yanshan Belt (YSB), itself located at the northern margin of the NCB ( Fig. 1 ; Davis et al., 2001; Zhao, 1990 ). To the north, the Xing- Meng suture (Suolon suture) indicates a ﬁnal closure of the Paleo- Asian ocean and the collision between the NCB and AMU during the Permian (Badarch et al., 2002; Li, 2006; Xiao et al., 2004; Yin and Nie, 1996). The YSB experienced vertical movements accompanied by intense deformation during the Mesozoic, including multiple generations of folds, thrusts and extensional faults (Davis et al., 2001; Zhao, 1990). In the Early Jurassic, a series of rift basins bounded by normal faulting were developed on the amalgamated NCB and AMU ( Darby et al., 2001; Meng, 2003; Zhao et al., 2002 ). From Early Jurassic to Early Cretaceous, extensive terrestrial volcanic and clastic sediments were deposited in these fault-related rift basins. These volcanic rocks, varying from ma ﬁc to intermediate- acid in composition, were genetically related to the process of lithospheric replacement beneath the NCB ( Zhang et al., 2003 ). The North and South China Blocks experienced counterclockwise and clockwise rotations during the welding event, respectively. The North China Block rotated counterclockwise by more than 60 ◦ rel- ative to the South China Block since Late Permian times about a pole of rotation located in the eastern part of the two blocks. The scissor-like process implied westward progression of the col- lision. Geological observations supported the westward closure of an ocean between the North and South China Blocks (Yin & Nie 1993). The former track is the largest segment in the Mesozoic apparent polar wander path for the North China Block: the palaeomagnetic poles for this block in the Early Triassic lie around 50–60 ◦N, 350◦E (Y anget al. 1991; Embleton et al. 1996), while those in the Middle and Late Jurassic fall around 70–80 ◦N, 220–230◦E (Y ang & Besse 2001). The pole position shifted by more than 40◦ in this period. Gilder & Courtillot (1997) interpreted that the termination of this earlier segment means cessation of the collision event and that the bulk of tectonic motion of the North China Block due to the collision occurred between the Early Triassic and Middle–Late Jurassic. Key words: Mesozoic, North China Block, palaeomagnetism, tectonics. 1 INTRODUCTION The North China Block and the South China Block are the major tectonic blocks forming East Asia (Fig. 1). The two blocks were located in distinct positions from each other through Precambrian– Palaeozoic times and were welded through a collision process in Early Mesozoic times. The collision of the North and South China Blocks is recognized by metamorphic belts observed between the two blocks. The Dabie Belt and the Sulu Belt that bound the two blocks yield coesite-bearing ultrahigh-pressure metamorphic rocks (Okay & S¸ eng¨or 1992). The Tan-Lu Fault also marks the bound- ary between the North and South China Blocks. This fault, to the north of the Dabie Belt and to the south of the Sulu Belt, marks the biogeographical and lithological boundary between the two blocks (Kobayashi 1967). Permian and Early Mesozoic palaeomagnetic data sets from the North and South China Blocks suggest that the two blocks su- tured following a scissor-like collision process (Zhao & Coe 1987). The North and South China Blocks experienced counterclockwise and clockwise rotations during the welding event, respectively. The Nor

e North China Block with respect to the South China Block during the welding event. At present, the Late Triassic and Early Jurassic representa- tive poles for the North China Block are based on palaeomagnetic data from a small number of studies (Y ang et al. 1991, 1992) that come from a single locality within the block (Ordos Basin, Fig. 1). The palaeomagnetic data of these important time periods have not been improved over the last decade. Attempts to accumulate reliable Triassic and Jurassic data have been thwarted by remagnetizations and lack of outcrops with good structural conditions to perform fold tests. As seen in the Early Jurassic demagnetization results of Y anget al. (1992), even successful palaeomagnetic works have encountered difﬁculties in isolating a high-ﬁdelity record of geo- magnetic ﬁeld directions in the North China Block, and a further study needs to be undertaken in order to contribute toward establish- ing representative Triassic and Jurassic poles for the North China Block. In this paper we present new palaeomagnetic results from Late Triassic and Early Jurassic rocks in the North China Block. This paper includes the ﬁrst report of a positive fold test for Early Jurassic rocks in the North China Block and improves the representative pole position in the Early Jurassic.

Received 2005 March 2; in original form 2004 February 2 SUMMARY Middle Triassic red-purple sandstones were sampled at four localities in the northeastern part of the South China Block (SCB) to detect regional deformational features. Twenty one sites consisting of 4 to 7 samples per site were drilled from the redbeds of the Middle Triassic Badong Formation from central Hubei province, China. These samples were subjected to progressive thermal demagnetization which revealed two components of magnetization. The low temperature (A) component was probably acq at a late stage of folding and is similar in direction to the late Mesozoic overprint widely observed in the eastern Yangtze Block . The high temperature (B ) component is Irefolding with dual polarity. Unlike the prefolding paleomagnetic directions observed in eastern Sichuan, western Hubei and northwestern Hunan, the B component resolved from central Hubei indicates no significant rotation with respect to other parts of the Yangtze Block. The Lower Red Unit (LRU) is mainly composed of siltstones, sandstones, acidic tuffs and red volca - niclastic microconglomerates. In the Cadí Basin, these lithologies interfinger with pyroclastic rocks that contain ignimbrites and inter - bedded banded rhyolites. Finally, the Upper Red Unit (URU) contains red conglomerates, sandstones, and siltstones ( Fig. 1 G) with carbonate nodules, and lacustrine deposits. These rocks are arranged in two se - quences, with interbedded volcanic bodies at the bottom. Mafic minerals and plagioclases in the volcanic series are replaced by opaque minerals, chlorite, ferromagnesian silicates, carbonates and sericite ( Gisbert, 1981 ; Bixel, 1984 ). Radiometric dating of extrusive rocks of the GU in the Cadí Basin yielded Late Carboniferous ages, including 304.0 ± 1.5 Ma (andesite) and 300.4 ± 1.4 Ma (ignimbrite) ( Pereira et al., 2014 ). 3. carrier_identity_candidates.excerpt: ona, Spain ARTICLE INFO Keywords: Paleomagnetism Volcanic Red beds Late Carboniferous Permian Pyrenees ABSTRACT We have carried out a detailed paleomagnetic study of volcanic rocks (18 sites) and red beds (10 sites) from the Late-Carboniferous-Permian series of the Cadí Basin (Eastern Pyrenees). The study provides reliable Late Carboniferous-Permian paleomagnetic directions, in an area where paleomagnetic studies are scarce. The main characteristic component in both rock types shows a SSE direction with a shallow inclination and a dominant reverse polarity. The magnetic carriers, both in the volcanic rocks and the red beds, are magnetite and hematite. The main component is interpreted as a primary magnetization of Permian age in the red beds; in the Late Carboniferous volcanic rocks, the main component likely represents primary magnetization or early remagne - tization. These results are consistent with the poles for the Iberian plate during the Permian and indicate an absence of regional vertical axis rotations for the Orri nappe, in whose hanging wall the Cadí Basin was trans - ported southwards during the Pyrenean orogeny. 1. The Lower Red Unit (LRU) is mainly composed of siltstones, sandstones, acidic tuffs and red volca - niclastic microconglomerates. In the Cadí Basin, these lithologies interfinger with pyroclastic rocks that contain ignimbrites and inter - bedded banded rhyolites. Finally, the Upper Red Unit (URU) contains red conglomerates, sandstones, and siltstones ( Fig. 1 G) with carbonate nodules, and lacustrine deposits. These rocks are arranged in two se - quences, with interbedded volcanic bodies at the bottom. Mafic minerals and plagioclases in the volcanic series are replaced by opaque minerals, chlorite, ferromagnesian silicates, carbonates and sericite ( Gisbert, 1981 ; Bixel, 1984 ). Radiometric dating of extrusive rocks of the GU in the Cadí Basin yielded Late Carboniferous ages, including 304.0 ± 1.5 Ma (andesite) and 300.4 ± 1.4 Ma (ignimbrite) ( Pereira et al., 2014 ). 3. This investigation was focus on the paleomagnetism of the Cretaceous marine sedi- mentary rocks, which will be a complement of paleo- magnetic data for unbalanced space distributions in the westernmost part of China [7]. More importantly, the sedimentary condition and tectonic background of ma- rine sediments in the SW Tarim are quite different from that of terrigenous sediments in north of Kuqa thrust depression, and hence, the paleomagnetic results of the marine sediments of SW Tarim are useful for discussion on red bed inclination shallowing and Cre- taceous tectonic evolution in Tarim. 1 Sampling The Cretaceous marine strata lie in the Tongyou- luke section near the Duoyunlike village, Akto County and this section is regarded as a standard profile of Cretaceous marine strata in SW Tarim [1]. The section we sampled concerns about 3000 m long and the geo- graphical position determined with a portable GPS at the bottom of the Cretaceous system is 38 °32′10″N, 76°14′27.6″E. The Sixes River terrane marks the northern- most tectonostratigraphic terrane in southwest- ern Oregon and is notably the product of ocean floor subduction (Blake et al., 1985). The ter - rane is divided into three fault-bounded belts of westward-younging Eocene mélange that con- tain high-grade blocks of Jurassic age (Coleman and Lanphere, 1971) and limestone blocks with Cenomanian microfossils ( Diller, 1898 ). The eastern and central mélange belts are overlain by middle Eocene Tyee Formation sandstones, while the western belt is overlapped by the sandstones of the Umpqua Group ( Figs. 2 and 3; see also Wiley et al., 2014). At Cape Blanco and Blacklock Point, these sandstones also overlie Late Jurassic rocks of the Gold Beach terrane, providing a minimum age of juxtaposi- tion of the Gold Beach terrane with southwest- ern Oregon (Fig. 3). Received 2011 February 15; in original form 2010 August 24 SUMMARY Shallow palaeomagnetic inclinations have been frequently reported from the red beds of central and southeast Asia. To trace the origin of this phenomenon, inclination variation in southeast Asia is examined on lithological to locality scale. Lithological aspect of this variation has been studied using the Early Cretaceous Bailong and Cangxi formations of the Bazhong area (32.1 ◦N, 106.7◦E), the northern Sichuan Basin. Although, inclination shallowing has not been detected in the coastal area of the SCB (Morinaga & Liu 2004; Zhu et al. 2006), anomalously large shallowing has been reported from the Sichuan Basin of the same block (Otofuji et al . 1990; Enkin et al. 1991a). Following these observations, demand for further in- vestigations became high to trace local origin of the inclination shallowing. Small-scale variation of inclination shallowing can be observed in the red beds strata, which mainly depends on the distribution of the size of grains and their ﬂocculated matters (ﬂocs) in the hematite bearing sediments as well as their mechanical compaction (Payen & V erosub 1982; Tanet al. 2002; Heslop 2007; Mitra & Tauxe 2009). Accordingly, lithological variation on strata scale could be taken as one of the targets in studying inclination shallowing. Palaeomagnetic study of the red beds on lithological to locality scale can give us a clue to investigate the origin of inclination shallowing. As a ﬁrst step in this procedure, palaeomagnetic study have been conducted to detect grain size dependence of inclination shallowing. L’âge de 426,4 6 2,0 Ma du gabbro de Mavillette est sensiblement plus jeune que le magmatisme vers 440 Ma, mais fait partie d ’une série déﬁnie par la géochimie de ﬁlons-couches et de roches volcaniques intra- plaques du Groupe de Rockville Notch, dont les âges vont jusqu ’au Dévonien précoce.
